newsitem.title: INDIA: Shy nun emerges from Mother Teresa's shadow.
newsitem.headline: Shy nun emerges from Mother Teresa's shadow.

text.p: Born a Hindu Brahmin, Sister Nirmala has quietly risen to the top of one of the most renowned Roman Catholic missions as the successor to an icon.
Soft-spoken and shy, Sister Nirmala had long stood in the shadow of Mother Teresa, a diminutive nun with a towering international stature.
But she emerged as the surprise choice to succeed the 86-year-old Nobel Prize winner on Thursday and asked for prayers to help her lead the Missionaries of Charity into a new era.
"I don't know how far I will be able to carry out the responsibility given to me. But I will try my best," Sister Nirmala told a crowd of journalists at the order's headquarters.
"Please pray for me," said the bespectacled nun, who favours the same style of white sari with blue trim worn by Mother Teresa.
Sister Nirmala's contradictions may have given her the critical edge against a half dozen other nuns who were possible successors to Mother Teresa without ever declaring their candidacies.
She was born a high-caste Hindu in 1934 from a family with its roots in Nepal -- the world's only Hindu kingdom.

Sister Nirmala's deceased father, Mahananda Joshi, served in the military police in the northern Indian state of Bihar, where Mother Teresa's successor was born. The oldest of 11 children, she travelled widely in India with her family as a child.
She earned a master's degree in political science before converting to Catholicism in 1958.
That year she joined the Calcutta-based mission that Mother Teresa had founded in 1948 and which has helped spread the Catholic church's message of care around the world.
Once in the order, Sister Nirmala studied law and was later sent to Panama where she ran the order's first mission house outside of India.
She later supervised the order's centres in Europe and the United States. Since 1979 she has led the mission's contemplative wing whose members dedicate their lives to meditation.
She was not one of the four councillors-general who head the organisation and thus was not considered a leading contender to replace Mother Teresa.
But her education, relatively young age, international exposure and rigorous intellectual devotion may have pushed her to the fore, church officials said.
The office of Calcutta Archbishop Henry D'Souza said the election of Nirmala after eight weeks of meditation and deliberation was "almost unanimous".
Until Thursday, Mother Teresa, born of Albanian parents, had won every previous election to the post of superior general of the order without losing a vote -- except her own.
While the nuns dashed speculation that they would choose a committee to take over from Mother Teresa, they stressed that the 86-year-old founder of the order would not slip into the shadows.

The Nobel Peace Prize winner, afflicted by heart, lung and kidney problems, will keep her name "Mother" even though Sister Nirmala will take over her administrative duties, Missionaries of Charity said.
"It's great that Sister Nirmala has been elected with God's will, but we will continue to have our Mother with us," said Sister Christine, one of the order's nuns.
"We get inspiration from her and I believe Sister Nirmala with her (Mother Teresa's) blessings will ably lead the organisation."
